The bleached, hardened stem with white mycelium strongly suggests Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot. Let me compare reference images one at a time across my top candidates.
Sclerotinia reference shows bleached stem at soil line with dark sclerotia. Similar bleaching but different location. Let me check Gray_Mold next.
Gray Mold shows tan-brown lesion with velvety gray spores at branch junction. The test image has more extensive bleaching and dryness. Let me check Alternaria stem cankers.
Alternaria shows dark brown canker, quite different from the bleached/gray appearance in the test image. Let me check Southern_Blight next.
Southern Blight shows white mycelium at soil line with soil attached. Different location and pattern from test image. Let me check more candidates.
Bacterial canker shows internal vascular discoloration on a cut stem. Very different from test image. Let me check Late_Blight and Bacterial_Wilt stems.
Late blight shows dark water-soaked stem lesion with white sporulation on green tissue. Very different from the bleached, dried test image. Two views left, need two more classes.
Bacterial wilt shows bacterial streaming test. Completely different. Last view.

The test image shows a stem canker at a branch junction that is **bleached, hardened, dried, and cracked** with patches of **white mycelium** visible. This matches Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot's key diagnostic features: "water-soaked areas that become covered with white cotton-like mycelium, bleached and hardened." The bleached, hardened quality of the tissue is the distinguishing feature from Gray Mold (which produces tan-brown lesions with velvety gray spore masses) and Rhizopus (which causes soft, watery decay with dense fuzzy coverage).
